plan.contextChunk: This figure contains four tall graduated cylinders arranged side by side on a common base labeled "Oil viscosity (SAE)," each filled with motor oil of a different SAE grade — 20, 30, 40, and 50 from left to right — and each holding a metal sphere dropped simultaneously from the top so that its position at a single elapsed moment reveals the oil's resistance to flow. The oils range progressively in color from pale yellow (SAE 20) to a deeper orange-red (SAE 50), and the position of the sphere descends less and less as the SAE grade increases: the sphere has fallen to the lower portion of the tube in grade 20, slightly higher in grade 30, noticeably higher in grade 40, and only to slightly above the midpoint of the column in grade 50. Because a more viscous fluid exerts a greater drag force on the sphere, slowing it to a lower terminal velocity, the shorter distance traveled in a fixed time directly encodes the ranking of viscosity across grades. The side-by-side format at a single instant converts viscosity — an intrinsic property — into a visually comparable positional difference, removing any need for stopwatches or calculations. This figure demonstrates viscosity as a rank-orderable physical property and establishes that higher SAE-grade oils offer greater internal resistance to the motion of an object moving through them.

elements: shared rectangular base slab (gold top face, red-trimmed front face) labeled 'Oil viscosity (SAE)'
four identical tall graduated cylinders standing vertically on the base, evenly spaced left-to-right
hexagonal/octagonal foot pedestal under each cylinder
pouring spout lip at the top rim of each cylinder
translucent glass wall of each cylinder (light blue-grey tint)
oil column inside each cylinder, color graded pale-yellow (SAE 20) to red-orange (SAE 50)
flat elliptical oil meniscus near the top of each column
one metallic grey sphere inside each cylinder at a grade-dependent height (lowest in SAE 20, highest in SAE 50)
numeric grade labels '20', '30', '40', '50' on the base front face beneath each cylinder
axis caption 'Oil viscosity (SAE)' centered on the base front face
terminal-velocity text labels that appear beside each sphere when toggled on

interactions.label: Drop all spheres
interactions.teaches: All four spheres released together fall at visibly different rates; the sphere in SAE 20 races to the bottom while the SAE 50 sphere barely descends, converting viscosity into a directly comparable positional difference at one instant

interactions.label: SAE grade
interactions.teaches: Dragging the grade continuously thickens the oil and slows a single probe sphere's descent, showing that terminal velocity decreases smoothly as viscosity increases rather than jumping between discrete grades

interactions.label: Terminal velocity labels
interactions.teaches: Once each sphere stops accelerating it descends at a constant terminal velocity; the labels reveal that this steady speed is inversely related to the oil's SAE grade

demo_steps.title: Release
demo_steps.narration: All four spheres start at the top of their columns at the same moment. The oils are colored from pale yellow (SAE 20) to red-orange (SAE 50).

demo_steps.title: Mid-descent ranking
demo_steps.narration: A short time later the SAE 20 sphere has dropped far while the SAE 50 sphere has moved little — the height gap at one instant ranks the viscosities without any stopwatch.

demo_steps.title: Steady descent with labels
demo_steps.narration: Each sphere now falls at its own constant terminal velocity. Turning on the labels shows the speed shrinking as the SAE grade rises.

demo_steps.title: Sweep one grade
demo_steps.narration: Use the SAE slider to thicken a single oil continuously and watch that probe sphere's fall slow smoothly, confirming the inverse viscosity–speed relationship between the discrete grades.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World layout: base slab ~8.0 (X) x 0.4 (Y height) x 2.2 (Z depth), centered at origin, top face at y=0. Four cylinders at x = -3.0, -1.0, +1.0, +3.0; each cylinder outer radius ~0.42, height ~4.0 standing on the base (y from 0 to 4.0) with a hexagonal foot pedestal ~0.55 radius x 0.25 tall and a small spout lip at the rim. Inner oil column radius ~0.34 filling y ~0.3 to ~3.6 with an elliptical meniscus at the top. Sphere radius ~0.34, metallic grey. Resting/illustrative sphere centers per grade (matching the source): SAE20 y~1.0, SAE30 y~1.5, SAE40 y~2.1, SAE50 y~2.6 (higher = less fallen). Oil colors: SAE20 #f1d98c, SAE30 #e9bd52, SAE40 #e69a5e, SAE50 #e05a48; glass tint #cfe0ea at ~0.25 opacity; base top #d9a83a, base front/edge trim #cc3322; grade text black. Illustrative terminal velocities for labels (cm/s): 20->3.0, 30->2.2, 40->1.5, 50->1.0; the slider interpolates speed ~ inversely with grade. Animation drops each sphere from y~3.4 to its grade rest height at a rate proportional to its terminal velocity, then loops.
interactionPlan.notes: Build each cylinder as an open-ended CylinderGeometry with a transparent MeshPhysicalMaterial (transmission/opacity ~0.25) for glass, plus a slightly smaller opaque cylinder for the oil and a CircleGeometry meniscus. Spheres use MeshStandardMaterial with metalness~0.9, roughness~0.3 and an environment map for the metallic highlight. Drive sphere y-position in the render loop from per-grade terminal velocity; the slider recomputes the probe sphere's velocity continuously. Velocity labels are camera-facing Sprites shown/hidden by the toggle. Keep all four reference tubes static in color/grade; the slider controls a single highlighted probe sphere (e.g. brighten its tube) so the race animation and the continuous sweep do not conflict.

authoredContext:
The test tubes shown here contain equal amounts of the specified motor oils. Identical metal spheres were dropped at the same time into each of the tubes, and a brief moment later, the spheres had fallen to the heights indicated in the illustration. Rank the motor oils in order of increasing viscosity, and explain your reasoning:

An image of four graduated cylinders sitting on a table labeled “Oil viscosity ( S A E )” is shown. The left-hand cylinder, labeled “20,” is mostly filled with light tan liquid and a metal ball is drawn in the lower fifth of the cylinder, but not on the bottom. The second cylinder, labeled “30,” is mostly filled with light brown liquid and a metal ball is drawn about three-fourths of the way down cylinder. The third cylinder, labeled “40,” is mostly filled with medium brown liquid and a metal ball is drawn halfway down the cylinder. The right-hand cylinder, labeled “50,” is mostly filled with brown liquid and a metal ball is drawn near the top of the liquid in the cylinder.

plan.authoredPrompt: This figure contains four tall graduated cylinders arranged side by side on a common base labeled "Oil viscosity (SAE)," each filled with motor oil of a different SAE grade — 20, 30, 40, and 50 from left to right — and each holding a metal sphere dropped simultaneously from the top so that its position at a single elapsed moment reveals the oil's resistance to flow. The oils range progressively in color from pale yellow (SAE 20) to a deeper orange-red (SAE 50), and the position of the sphere descends less and less as the SAE grade increases: the sphere has fallen to the lower portion of the tube in grade 20, slightly higher in grade 30, noticeably higher in grade 40, and only to slightly above the midpoint of the column in grade 50. Because a more viscous fluid exerts a greater drag force on the sphere, slowing it to a lower terminal velocity, the shorter distance traveled in a fixed time directly encodes the ranking of viscosity across grades. The side-by-side format at a single instant converts viscosity — an intrinsic property — into a visually comparable positional difference, removing any need for stopwatches or calculations. This figure demonstrates viscosity as a rank-orderable physical property and establishes that higher SAE-grade oils offer greater internal resistance to the motion of an object moving through them.

- Slider for oil SAE grade (20 to 50): watch a single ball's drop rate slow continuously as viscosity increases
- Toggle to display terminal velocity labels on each ball once each sphere reaches steady descent speed
